   Therefore, $p_{A^T}(\lambda) = p_A(\lambda)$ for all $\lambda$.

   Since the characteristic polynomials are identical, their roots (which are the eigenvalues) are the same.
   Hence, the set of eigenvalues of $A$ (i.e., $\sigma(A)$) is equal to the set of eigenvalues of $A^T$ (i.e., $\sigma(A^T)$).

Consider the characteristic polynomial of $A^T$:  
$$\det(A^T - \lambda I).$$  
By Assumption 2, we have:  
$$\det(A^T - \lambda I) = \det((A - \lambda I)^T) = \det(A - \lambda I),$$  
where the last equality holds because the determinant of a matrix equals the determinant of its transpose.  

Thus, $\det(A^T - \lambda I) = \det(A - \lambda I)$ for all $\lambda$. Consequently, $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ if and only if:  
$$\det(A - \lambda I) = 0 \iff \det(A^T - \lambda I) = 0,$$  
meaning $\lambda$ is also an eigenvalue of $A^T$. Therefore, the sets of eigenvalues are identical: $\sigma(A) = \sigma(A^T)$.
